newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Duma gives nod to tax code as Yeltsin heads for G7.
newsitem.headline: Duma gives nod to tax code as Yeltsin heads for G7.

text.p: Russia's communist-dominated parliament gave in on Thursday to strong pressure from the government and tentatively approved a draft tax code which ministers say is crucial to reforms.

This should come as a good news for President Boris Yeltsin who left on Thursday for a summit with the Group of Seven leaders in the United States which will provide an opportunity for him to bask in the spotlight of the world media.
The Kremlin said Yeltsin told a group of reporters before leaving that he would not, however, be attending the July summit of NATO states in Madrid.

The Madrid summit is awkward for Moscow because it is expected to take a decision on inviting some east European countries to join, a move Russia, which signed a cooperation deal with NATO in May, sees as damaging its security interests.

Ministers say the draft tax code discussed by parliament on Thursday is crucial to future budgets, helping to cut domestic producers' tax burden, stabilise the tax system and decrease tax pressure on private individuals.

In the Duma, 254 deputies backed a resolution passing the code in the first reading. Only 84 voted against. The resolution contains several clauses designed to help the Duma save face and says the second reading of the bill should start on November 1.
The draft suggests cutting the number of tax groups of Russian citizens and businesses to 28 from 75.
As a result the government will lose 73-75 trillion roubles ($12.6-$13 billion), but enterprises would save money and be able to make greater investment, ministers say.

Private individuals will pay a 30 percent income tax on annual earnings of more than 60 million roubles and only 12 percent on anything below that level. Russia is currently using a five-grade tax system with a top rate of 35 percent.
The government has said the 1998 budget may be in jeopardy unless the Duma gives initial backing to the code before its summer recess and have applied a carrot-and-stick policy.
Earlier this week the cabinet offered the Duma a compromise, allowing deputies until September to present amendments once the code passes the first reading.

At the same time First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, Russia's reform guru, hinted the Duma might regret not backing the government on what he called "the issue of issues" and said: "We consider the Thursday vote to be decisive".

Both government and opposition have denied rumours of a secret deal under which the Communists would back the draft while ministers would stop mentioning the possiblity of Yeltsin dissolving the legislature.
The Thursday vote somewhat equalled the score in the stand-off between the cabinet and the deputies.
On Tuesday the Duma threw out a package of bills to reduce or scrap most Soviet-era welfare benefits, which the cabinet says have become too heavy a burden for the new Russia.
The cuts would mostly affect the poor and elderly -- the main electorate of the opposition.

On Wednesday, the Duma again stalled a government plan to cut spending in the 1997 budget, but the government has said that the cuts will go ahead irrespective of the vote. The Duma will consider its own budget-cutting plan on Friday.
